film.bigQuestion: If you found a rock with a fish shape pressed into it, in the middle of dry land, what would that tell you about what that place was like long ago?

captions.text: This is Wyoming. Dry, dusty land, with hardly any water.
But hidden in this rock is something surprising...
About 52 million years ago, this land was a warm lake. Fish swam everywhere.
Palm trees grew along its shore.
Layer by layer, mud buried them. Slowly, the mud turned to stone.
Today, scientists dig up these clues. Some even dive for them, right here in Florida.
Every fossil is a message from long ago. Let's learn to read it.

words: What is left of a living thing from long ago, like a bone, shell, or footprint in rock.
Information that helps explain something. Scientists use evidence, not guessing.
No longer living anywhere on Earth. Dinosaurs are extinct.
The place where a living thing lives: the land, water, air, plants, and animals around it.
To use clues to figure something out. It is careful thinking, not guessing.
Any living thing: a plant, an animal, or even a tiny germ.

parts.title: Fossils Are Clues in Stone
parts.html:
A fossil is what is left of a living thing from long, long ago. Bones, shells, leaves, and even footprints can become fossils.

Fossils hold clues, like the shape of a fin or the lines in a leaf. Each clue is a piece of evidence.

parts.title: Fossils Tell Us About Ancient Living Things
parts.html:
Scientists look closely at a fossil's shape. A fish fossil with fins and a backbone shows what the fish looked like and how it swam. A tooth's shape tells what an animal ate. When scientists use clues like these to figure something out, they infer.

Many of these living things are extinct. None are alive anywhere on Earth today. Fossils are the only way we know they lived.

parts.title: Fossils Tell Us About Ancient Places
parts.html:
Here is a surprise: scientists have found sea shells on mountaintops and fish in dry deserts. That is not a mistake. It is evidence that those places were very different long ago.

A fossil tells you about its environment. A fern fossil means the land was warm and wet. A coral fossil means warm, shallow sea water once covered that spot.

order.title: How does a fish become a fossil?
order.look: Four real photos. Each one shows one scene from a fossil's story, but they are mixed up. The dark film strip has four empty frames, from first (1) to last (4).
order.done: 🎬 Your order is right. Now watch it as a movie!

check.q: Look at scene 3 again. The fish's bones are now…

options.t: still soft bone, just like a fish today.
options.miss: Not quite. Bones that sit in rock for millions of years don't stay soft. Look at scene 3: it is hard rock.

options.t: stone in the shape of the bones.
options.ok: Yes! Water with tiny bits of rock soaked in and slowly filled the shape. The fossil is rock in the shape of the bones.

options.t: gone, with nothing left at all.
options.miss: Not quite. If nothing were left, there would be no fossil to find. Look at scene 3 again.

beats.cap: 1 · A fish dies and sinks to the bottom of the lake.
2 · Mud and sand drift down and cover it.
3 · Layer after layer piles on top. Time passes…
4 · The soft parts are gone. Rock has filled in the shape of the bones.

compare.title: What can a tooth's shape tell us?
compare.look: Two real fossil teeth from two extinct animals, each on a lit specimen tray. A tooth's shape is a clue to the job it did. Under the trays are test materials for a model: a real leaf and a strip of soft clay.

trays.alt: A large dark fossil back tooth with bumps on top
trays.label: Specimen B

ask.q: Which tooth looks better for crushing?
ask.ok: Yes. Specimen B is wide with round bumps, good for crushing.
ask.miss: Look at the tops. Which one is wide with bumps for crushing?

ask.q: Which tooth looks better for slicing?
ask.ok: Yes. Specimen A is pointy with sharp edges, good for slicing.
ask.miss: Look at the edges. Which one is pointy and sharp?

compare.testDo: Drag the leaf onto one tray and the clay strip onto the other (or tap a material, then tap a tray). Then press Press down.
compare.disclaimer: This is a model. It shows how a tooth's shape can match its job. It is not proof of exactly what each animal ate.

Bleaf.text: The wide, bumpy tooth crushed the leaf flat. Crushing breaks up tough plants.

Aleaf.text: The sharp tooth poked holes and tore the leaf, but it didn't grind it up.

Aclay.text: The sharp edge sliced right through the clay strip.

Bclay.text: The bumpy tooth squashed the clay, but it didn't cut it.

compare.frame: This ___ has ___, so I think the animal probably ate ___.
compare.claimMid: so I think the animal probably ate

curator.A: Sharp slicing edges → likely a meat eater. Specimen A is a tooth from megalodon, a giant shark. Megalodon is extinct. Teeth like this are found in Florida rivers.
curator.B: Wide grinding top → likely a plant eater. Specimen B is a back tooth from a mastodon, an animal like an elephant. Mastodons are extinct. Their bones have been found in Florida springs.

compare.missFeat: Look at the tooth on {label} again. What shape do you see?
compare.missClaim: Think about your test. What did this shape do best?
compare.done: Shape can tell us about function (the job a part does). That helps scientists infer how extinct animals lived.

after.alt: A dark fossil trilobite with many body segments
after.html: This is a trilobite. Trilobites lived in the sea for about 270 million years. Then every last one died out. They are extinct, so fossils are the only way we know they lived.

wall.title: Read the Grand Canyon like a book
wall.look: A cutaway (a slice) of a cliff, like the walls of the Grand Canyon. It is a model of four real rock layers. A real fossil found in each layer is hidden under the dust. The brass dial on the left is a time elevator. It shows how far back in time you are.
wall.do: First, make a prediction. Then brush the glowing layer: drag across it (or tap it again and again) until the fossil shows.

predict.q: Which layer do you think formed first, long, long ago?
predict.mine: Your prediction: the {p} layer formed first. Let's dig and find out.
predict.confirm: You predicted the bottom layer formed first. The evidence agrees.
predict.change: You predicted the top layer. The evidence changed that idea: the bottom layer formed first, so it is the oldest.

wall.locked: Clear the layer above first. It sits on top, so you reach it first.
wall.first: Brush the glowing top layer. Drag across it (or tap it again and again).
wall.next: Going deeper, and farther back in time. Brush Layer {n}.
wall.endText: Look at the line on the cliff. It runs from the oldest layer at the bottom to the youngest at the top.
wall.rule: In this undisturbed rock column, the lower layers formed first. Undisturbed means nothing flipped or mixed the layers.

layers.ask: Look at the fossil from Layer 1. What was this place like when it lived?
layers.clue: A shell with ribs, called a brachiopod. Animals with shells like this live in the sea today.
layers.ok: Yes! A sea animal means this place was under the sea.

miss.1: Look at the clue: shells like this live in the sea, not in sand dunes.
miss.2: Ferns don't have shells. Read the clue again.

layers.alt: Small footprints pressed into tan sandstone
layers.ask: Now Layer 2. What was this place like?
layers.clue: Tiny footprints in sandstone. Sandstone is made of grains of sand pressed together. Animals walked across these sand hills.
layers.ok: Yes! Footprints across sand hills mean this place was a desert of sand dunes.

miss.0: Footprints are made by walking on dry ground. Read the clue again.

layers.alt: A fern leaf print in red rock
layers.ask: Now Layer 3. What was this place like?

miss.1: Ferns need water, so this was not a dry desert. Read the clue again.

layers.ask: Last one: Layer 4, at the very bottom. What was this place like?
layers.clue: A trilobite. Trilobite fossils are always found with other sea animals.
layers.ok: Yes! The sea was here too, a very, very long time ago.

miss.1: Trilobites lived with other sea animals, not in dry sand. Read the clue again.
miss.2: Trilobites lived with other sea animals, not on land. Read the clue again.

mix.q: Layer 1 holds a sea animal. Layer 2, right under it, was a desert of sand dunes. Did the sea animals crawl into the desert?

options.t: Yes. The sea animals moved into the desert.
options.miss: Sea animals can't live in a dry desert. Look at the order: the desert layer is under the sea layer, so the desert was there first.

options.t: No. The place changed. First it was a desert. Later, the sea covered it.
options.ok: Yes! The animals didn't move. The PLACE changed. First it was a desert. Much later, the sea covered it.

wow.title: The top of the world was once the sea floor
wow.alt: Mount Everest, a huge snowy mountain under a blue sky
wow.caption: Mount Everest, the tallest mountain on Earth.
wow.html:
The rock at the very top of Mount Everest is limestone, a rock that forms in the sea. Scientists have found fossils of sea animals in it, including trilobites.

Very slowly, over millions of years, that old sea floor was pushed up into the sky.

keyIdea: Fossils are evidence. They show what living things looked like and where they lived, even if those living things are extinct and those places have changed. In undisturbed rock, deeper layers hold older fossils.

quiz.q: A scientist finds a fossil of a coral reef creature in a dry desert. What does this evidence most likely tell us?

options.t: The organism crawled out of the ocean to live in the desert.
options.miss: Think about what coral needs to live. Corals only grow in sea water. What does that tell you about the desert long ago?

options.t: The desert was once covered by a warm, shallow ocean.
options.ok: 🌊 Exactly! The fossil is evidence of a past environment. That place used to be very different.

options.t: Coral can survive without water in dry environments.
options.miss: Coral can't live without water. Corals only grow in sea water. What does that tell you about the desert long ago?

quiz.q: Which best describes what it means to infer something from a fossil?

options.t: Making a wild guess about what it looked like.
options.miss: Inferring is not guessing. Scientists use clues they can see, like size and shape.

options.t: Copying information from another scientist's notes.
options.miss: Copying isn't inferring. Inferring means using clues you can see yourself, like size and shape.

options.t: Using specific clues in the fossil to reach a careful explanation.
options.ok: 🌿 That's it! Inferring is careful thinking with evidence. Scientists use clues like size, shape, and parts.

quiz.q: Scientists find two fossils in the same place, one deeper in the rock than the other. What can they infer about the two fossils?

options.t: The deeper fossil is older. It lived before the organism in the upper layer.
options.ok: ⭐ Excellent! Deeper layers formed first, so fossils there lived longer ago. That's how scientists build a timeline of life.

options.t: The upper fossil is older because it's closer to the surface.
options.miss: Rock layers stack up like a pile of blankets. The one on the bottom was put down first.

options.t: Both organisms lived at exactly the same time.
options.miss: Rock layers stack up one at a time, like a pile of blankets. Layers at different depths formed at different times.

partA.title: Match fossils to evidence
partA.do: Read each fossil clue. Pick the best answer, or type your answer.

items.q: A fish fossil with fins and a backbone is found in dry, rocky ground. Where did this fish most likely live long ago?

options.t: In water, like a lake or ocean
options.ok: Yes. Fins and a backbone are clues for swimming, so it lived in water.

options.t: In a forest
options.miss: Fish need water. Which choice has water?

options.t: In a desert
options.miss: That's where it was FOUND. Fish need water. Where did it LIVE?

items.q: A large curved tooth with sharp ridges is found deep underground. What does the tooth's shape tell you about how the animal got its food?
chips: Says what it ate or how it got food

items.q: A leaf fossil with thick veins and a wide shape is found in rock. What kind of climate does this plant fossil show?

options.t: Hot and wet
options.ok: Yes. Big, wide leaves grow where it is warm and wet.

options.t: Cold and dry
options.miss: Big, wide leaves need lots of water and warmth. Try again.

options.t: Sandy and dry
options.miss: Big, wide leaves need lots of water. Sandy, dry places have very little.
